howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: McAfee Station on the Salt River
stories.summary: In May 1773, Virginia’s McAfee Company—brothers James, Robert, and George, with James McCoun Jr. and Samuel Adams—surveyed fertile Salt River bottomlands in…
stories.place: McAfee Station on the Salt River
stories.quote: In May 1773, Virginia’s McAfee Company—brothers James, Robert, and George, with James McCoun Jr. and Samuel Adams—surveyed fertile Salt River bottomlands in today’s Mercer County.

photo.title: New Providence Presbyterian Church near Salvisa — grew from the McAfee Station community (1785)
photo.attribution: Flynnke · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

stories.title: Washington, Mason County
stories.summary: In 1785 Arthur Fox and Baptist preacher William Wood bought about 700 acres and laid out a one-mile-square town; Virginia chartered Washington in 1786—widely cited as the first…
stories.quote: In 1785 Arthur Fox and Baptist preacher William Wood bought about 700 acres and laid out a one-mile-square town; Virginia chartered Washington in 1786—widely cited as the first American settlement named for George Washington while Kentucky was still part of Virginia.

photo.title: Paxton Inn in Old Washington (Washington Historic District, now Maysville)
photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

stories.title: Blue Jacket (Weyapiersenwah)
stories.summary: Shawnee war chief Blue Jacket (c. 1743–1810) first appears in written records at his Scioto town in 1773, fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore’s War, and allied with the…
stories.quote: Shawnee war chief Blue Jacket (c. 1743–1810) first appears in written records at his Scioto town in 1773, fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore’s War, and allied with the British through the Revolution.

photo.title: Treaty of Greenville (1795) — Blue Jacket among Shawnee leaders who signed after Fallen Timbers
photo.attribution: Artist unknown (c. 1795) · Wikimedia Commons · public domain

stories.title: Slone Site (15Pi11), Pike County
stories.summary: On the north bank of the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, Slone was a late Middle Fort Ancient circular village occupied about 1350–1400 CE for roughly thirty to forty-five years.…
stories.quote: On the north bank of the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, Slone was a late Middle Fort Ancient circular village occupied about 1350–1400 CE for roughly thirty to forty-five years.

layers.blurb: Daniel Boone’s 1775 settlement on the Kentucky River — Capital of the Colony of Transylvania.

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

photo.title: Big Bone Lick State Park
photo.attribution: Mattguyver · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

layers.name: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.attribution: Lee Wright · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

layers.name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
layers.wiki: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park
layers.blurb: The Sinking Spring farm where Lincoln was born in 1809, plus the Knob Creek boyhood unit.

photo.title: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace memorial
photo.attribution: Jon698 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

photo.title: Blue Licks Battlefield monument
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

photo.title: Old Talbott Tavern, Bardstown
photo.attribution: Christopher L. Riley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.title: Goddard Covered Bridge
photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.title: Kentucke Gazette printing house
photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.title: Cumberland Falls
photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.

photo.title: Frankfort Cemetery
photo.attribution: Sydney Poore & Russell Poore · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Buffalo Trace Distillery
layers.blurb: A Kentucky River distilling campus with late-1700s roots, continuous through Prohibition.

photo.attribution: Kittugwiki · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0
